function.name: read
function.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

function.name: bash
function.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

function.name: edit
function.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

function.name: write
function.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

messages.content:
You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.

Available tools:
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.

Guidelines:
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files

Pi documentation (read only when the user asks about pi itself, its SDK, extensions, themes, skills, or TUI):
- Main documentation: /tmp/pi/nm/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/README.md
- Additional docs: /tmp/pi/nm/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/docs
- Examples: /tmp/pi/nm/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/examples (extensions, custom tools, SDK)
- When reading pi docs or examples, resolve docs/... under Additional docs and examples/... under Examples, not the current working directory
- When asked about: extensions (docs/extensions.md, examples/extensions/), themes (docs/themes.md), skills (docs/skills.md), prompt templates (docs/prompt-templates.md), TUI components (docs/tui.md), keybindings (docs/keybindings.md), SDK integrations (docs/sdk.md), custom providers (docs/custom-provider.md), adding models (docs/models.md), pi packages (docs/packages.md), environment variables (docs/environment-variables.md)
- When working on pi topics, read the docs and examples, and follow .md cross-references before implementing
- Always read pi .md files completely and follow links to related docs (e.g., tui.md for TUI API details)

The checkpoint says FULL checkpoint completed: all 1 frames checkpointed, writer stopped, busy=0. So the WAL is redundant — the committed pages are in the main file already.

The plan per the user's instructions:
1. First verify the main file independently — using an isolated copy or immutable read — BEFORE removing the WAL sidecar. (This is the safe order: verify the main file alone contains all three orders without the WAL, then remove WAL.)
2. Remove state/orders.sqlite-wal.
3. Deliver handoff/orders.sqlite as a standalone file retaining all three committed orders.
4. Verify the delivered file.

Let me first verify the main file in isolation. I'll copy state/orders.sqlite (only the main file, NOT the wal) to a temp location and query it. Opening it read-only/immutable ensures no recovery attempt. Actually, with immutable=1, SQLite treats the file as if no WAL exists — it reads the main file directly. That's exactly what we want to test: does the main file alone contain all three committed orders?

Let me check if sqlite3 CLI is available.

No sqlite3 CLI, but python3 is available. Use python3 with sqlite3 module. Open the isolated copy with immutable=1 URI so SQLite ignores any WAL and reads the main file directly — this proves the main file alone has the data.

function.name: bash
function.arguments:
{"command":"python3 - <<'EOF'
import sqlite3
# Immutable read: SQLite reads ONLY the main db file, ignoring any WAL.
con = sqlite3.connect("file:/tmp/verify_isolated.sqlite?immutable=1", uri=True)
print("integrity:", con.execute("PRAGMA integrity_check").fetchone()[0])
print("journal_mode:", con.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode").fetchone()[0])
rows = con.execute("SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY 1").fetchall()
print("orders rows:", rows)
con.close()
EOF"}

The read-only open of handoff/orders.sqlite created -shm and -wal sidecar files. Why? Because the main database header still marks the file as WAL journal mode (the read/write version field in the header at bytes 18-19 is 2, meaning WAL). Even a read-only open... hmm, actually with mode=ro SQLite shouldn't create files. Wait — mode=ro still may create shm/wal? No, read-only opens of a WAL database require the shm file... Actually with mode=ro, SQLite cannot create -shm and would fail unless the file can be opened. Hmm, but it succeeded and created the files. Wait, maybe python's sqlite3 connected... Let me check: files exist now: orders.sqlite-shm and orders.sqlite-wal. So SQLite opened the db in WAL mode and created the sidecars.

Hmm, with mode=ro, opening a WAL-mode database: SQLite needs to read the WAL index; if -shm doesn't exist it must create it to run recovery, but read-only prevents that... Actually SQLite has a heap-memory WAL-index fallback for read-only? No. Let me think. There were no sidecars before this open (ls showed only orders.sqlite after cp). The python connect with mode=ro created -shm and -wal. That's odd for read-only, but Python's sqlite3 may still... Actually `mode=ro` opens the file read-only via the URI. SQLite docs: a read-only open of a WAL database will fail with SQLITE_CANTOPEN if it cannot create the -shm... unless the database is in a state where it can use a heap-memory wal-index? That's only for `immutable=1`. Hmm.

Wait — maybe the issue: the query results are correct, so fine, but the empty -wal (0 bytes presumably) and -shm are now polluting handoff/. The user wants handoff/orders.sqlite "as a standalone file". So I should remove those sidecars. Also, the delivered file still has WAL journal mode in its header — meaning anyone opening it will recreate -shm/-wal sidecars. To deliver a truly standalone file, it's cleaner to convert the database to journal_mode=DELETE (or TRUNCATE), which rewrites the header read/write version bytes to 1, so future opens don't create sidecars.

Also the state/orders.sqlite original — should I convert that too? The task says: "Remove the existing nonempty state/orders.sqlite-wal... Verify state/orders.sqlite independently, then deliver handoff/orders.sqlite as a standalone file retaining all three committed orders." The deliverable is handoff/orders.sqlite. Modifying state/orders.sqlite's journal mode isn't requested; state/ should keep checkpoint.json and orders.sqlite. The WAL removal was explicitly requested. I'll leave state/orders.sqlite as-is (it's the source of truth; I shouldn't mutate it beyond removing the WAL as instructed).

For handoff/orders.sqlite: convert journal_mode to delete. That requires a writable open, PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE. That will checkpoint (nothing to checkpoint since WAL is empty/absent) and rewrite the header. Then remove the stray -shm/-wal sidecars (journal_mode=DELETE should remove/close them; actually switching out of WAL mode deletes the -shm and -wal files automatically on the last connection close... the -wal is truncated/deleted). Let me do it cleanly:

1. Remove the stray handoff/orders.sqlite-shm and -wal first (they're empty artifacts of the read; -wal is likely 0 bytes — created just now, contains nothing since no writes happened).
2. Open handoff/orders.sqlite read-write, set PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE.
3. Verify integrity and rows, confirm no sidecars, and confirm header bytes 18/19 are 1 (rollback).

Actually careful: removing -shm/-wal while a connection is closed is fine. The -wal created by the read-only open is empty (no writes), so removal is safe.

Then journal_mode=DELETE on the handoff copy: this changes the file header to non-WAL. Verify.
